Nov 12 : Manchester United sacked manager Michael Carrick on Thursday after an eight-game winless Premier League run. The 45-year-old was their seventh permanent boss since Alex Ferguson retired after guiding the club to their last league title in 2013. Following is a list of permanent and interim managers who have taken charge at United following Ferguson's retirement: David Moyes In charge: July 1, 2013-April 22, 2014 (10 months)

Matches: 51 Win-Draw-Loss: 27-9-15 Trophies won: 1 (Community Shield) Former Everton manager Moyes struggled to fill Ferguson's shoes as defending champions United suffered with inconsistency, finishing seventh in the Premier League. Ryan Giggs (caretaker) In charge: April 22, 2014-May 11, 2014 (1 month) Matches: 4 Win-Draw-Loss: 2-1-1 Trophies won: 0 It was the first major coaching assignment for United's former midfielder Giggs, who holds the club's appearance record of 963. He remained at United as an assistant coach until 2016. Louis van Gaal In charge: July 16, 2014-May 23, 2016 (22 months) Matches: 103 Win-Draw-Loss: 54-25-24 Trophies won: 1 (FA Cup) Dutchman Van Gaal arrived at United as one of the most respected managers of his generation, with successful spells at Barcelona, Bayern Munich, Ajax Amsterdam and the Netherlands over two decades. United's performances improved and they finished fourth in 2014-15. But Van Gaal's possession-heavy playing style was criticised and he was fired two days after winning the FA Cup. Jose Mourinho In charge: May 27, 2016-December 18, 2018 (31 months) Matches: 144 Win-Draw-Loss: 84-32-28 Trophies won: 3 (Europa League, League Cup, Community Shield) Mourinho's arrival reflected United's ambition and his tenure got off to an optimistic start, with the team winning the League Cup and Europa League in his first campaign, followed by a second-place finish in the Premier League the next season. Despite United spending nearly £400 million ($534.28 million) on players, a drop in performances in 2018-19 led to his dismissal when the team were 19 points off top spot. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer In charge: December 19, 2018 (On interim basis, made permanent in March 2019) - November 21, 2021 (35 months) Matches: 168 Win-Draw-Loss: 91-37-40 Trophies won: 0 Former United forward Solskjaer coached the club's reserve side from 2008-2011. He also managed Cardiff City and Norwegian club Molde before being appointed United's interim boss. Solskjaer won 14 of his 19 matches before being made permanent manager but inconsistency plagued United for the rest of his stay. The Norwegian was dismissed after a string of losses including against Liverpool, Manchester City and Watford. Michael Carrick (caretaker) In charge: November 21, 2021-December 2, 2021 (12 days) Matches: 3 Win-Draw-Loss: 2-1-0 Former United midfielder Carrick was part of the club's coaching staff when appointed caretaker manager for less than two weeks, marking the start of his managerial career. Ralf Rangnick (interim) In charge: Dec. 3, 2021-May 22, 2022 (6 months) Matches: 29 Win-Draw-Loss: 11-10-8 Trophies won: 0 Rangnick attempted to steady the ship during a difficult season with underwhelming results as United came sixth in the Premier League and exited the Champions League in the last 16. Erik ten Hag In charge: May 23, 2022-October 28, 2024 (29 months) Matches: 128 Win-Draw-Loss: 70-23-35 Trophies won: 2 (FA Cup, League Cup) Ten Hag arrived at United following a successful spell at Ajax but, despite winning the League Cup and securing a top-four finish in his first season, his tenure took a downward turn. United came eighth in 2023-24 but the Dutchman was given a second chance after winning the FA Cup. United were sitting 14th in October 2024 when he was fired. Ruud van Nistelrooy (interim) In charge: October 28, 2024 - November 10, 2024 (13 days) Matches: 4 Win-Draw-Loss: 3-1-0 Former United and Netherlands striker Van Nistelrooy, who joined the club as an assistant coach in July 2024, went unbeaten in four matches in all competitions as interim boss. Ruben Amorim In charge: November 11, 2024 - January 5, 2026 (14 months) Matches: 63 Win-Draw-Loss: 25-15-23 Trophies won: 0 Amorim, who led Sporting to two Primeira Liga titles, had an unwavering commitment to an expansive 3-4-3 system built on intense pressing and possession-based football. The 39-year-old became United's youngest manager since Wilf McGuinness took charge at 31 in 1969, but his spell ended after a poor run of results and public clashes. Darren Fletcher (Interim) In charge: January 5, 2026 - January 13, 2026 (9 days) Matches: 2 Win-Draw-Loss: 0-1-1 Former United player Fletcher took charge of two matches, a Premier League draw with Burnley and an FA Cup defeat by Brighton & Hove Albion. Michael Carrick In Charge: January 13, 2026 - November 12, 2026 (10 months) Matches: 29 Win-Draw-Loss: 14-7-8 Trophies won: 0 Former United and England midfielder Carrick was appointed on an interim basis before being handed a contract until 2028 after winning 11 of his first 16 matches. Under Carrick, United climbed to third in the top flight and secured qualification for the Champions League. However, he proved unable to carry that momentum into the new season and was dismissed after an eight-game Premier League winless streak. ($1 = 0.7487 pounds)

Source: Reuters

Nov 12 : New Zealand's Liam Lawson and Britain's Arvid Lindblad will continue with Racing Bulls next season, the Red Bull-owned Formula One team said on Thursday. The announcement ends speculation about Lawson's future with the team. "I have no doubt that this is the best driver line-up for us, bringing a strong combination of experience and ambition," said team principal Alan Permane in a statement. Lawson has scored 75 of Racing Bulls' 114 points in 20 races so far this season, with the team currently fifth overall. His place was uncertain, however, with 19-year-old Bulgarian junior driver Nikola Tsolov also linked to the seat.

Source: Reuters

PARIS, Nov 12 : France's armed forces ministry said on Thursday it will create an international centre to promote and support the growing use of artificial intelligence in defence, as Europe races to strengthen its military technology capabilities and reduce its reliance on the United States. The ministry is hoping that NATO will recognise the centre, due to open in summer 2027, an official told reporters at a briefing. AI tools have become key to warfare since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, helping to speed up battlefield decision-making by processing and interpreting large quantities of data produced by drones, satellites and other sensors. However, Europe is reliant on US-based companies like Palantir for much of its AI-enabled military software.  The ministry has not yet finalised funding or international members for the centre. It has invited representatives from other countries to a conference next week to outline its plans for the initiative.

Source: Reuters

FAST

Nov 12 : Manchester United's decision to sack Michael Carrick on Thursday after another dismal run feels like a familiar episode in the post-Alex Ferguson era, but the latest managerial departure raises deeper questions about the team's underlying problems. Three wins from 15 games in all competitions, the worst defensive record in Europe and a side in the relegation zone are statistics that would test the patience of any club hierarchy and leave few managers with a realistic chance of survival. But the fundamental question remains: whether the Old Trafford side's problems lie in the dugout or in a club that has repeatedly chosen to change their head coach. Carrick is the seventh permanent manager to be sacked by the United hierarchy since Ferguson clinched the club's 20th league title and retired in 2013. He is also the third to be sacked since Jim Ratcliffe came on board as a minority owner in 2024.

In the last 13 years, the club have consumed reputations by cycling through big names like David Moyes, Louis van Gaal, Jose Mourinho and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer while remaining convinced that the next appointment will make it all work. What made Carrick's tenure remarkable is his rise and fall - how convincingly things worked last term before the subsequent decline that showed he was unable to sustain the momentum that propelled him from interim to permanent manager. Appointed after Ruben Amorim's departure, Carrick's side won 11 of his first 16 games in charge, beating Arsenal, Manchester City, Liverpool and Chelsea while lifting United into the Champions League places last season. But that initial recovery - seen before with managers like his former teammate Solskjaer - was mistaken by the club's hierarchy as evidence the team's deeper problems were solved. Managers have arrived at Old Trafford with different philosophies, personalities and promises. But the common denominator is the club that hired them, backed them and eventually discarded them. CARRICK INVITED SCRUTINY There is a legitimate case against Carrick as his team's defensive organisation has been poor, performances deteriorated and his handling of Bruno Fernandes - particularly the decision to bench the captain against Bournemouth - invited scrutiny. But even the sharpest tactical mind can only mask structural shortcomings for so long and no amount of ingenuity can indefinitely compensate for poor squad building. United remain one of the world's wealthiest clubs and have never been short of financial muscle, but there is a vast difference between spending heavily and spending wisely. Their summer outlay of £150 million ($198.86 million) was committed solely to midfield, with Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans arriving. Yet significant weaknesses in the squad were left unaddressed, most notably at left back. The lack of strategic squad planning was laid bare by the fact that a team competing on four fronts had only the injury-prone 31-year-old Luke Shaw as an established senior left back. Meanwhile, a succession of signings tailored to the short-term needs of individual managers has left United with a costly and often disjointed squad, forcing each new coach to work with players recruited for vastly different tactical approaches. Without a clear footballing identity shaping recruitment, the incoming manager - with US coach Mauricio Pochettino likely to replace Carrick - risks inheriting the same structural flaws. ($1 = 0.7543 pounds)

Source: Reuters

Nov 12 : The autumn rout in AI stocks has reset the market for convertible securities often used by technology firms keen to raise funds cheaply, in a development that has investors breathing a sigh of relief.  A wave of convertible issues this week bears terms that more evenly balance the priorities of fundraising companies with those of investors who want to participate in further stock-market rallies, analysts said.  Dropbox's $1.1 billion convertible offering, priced on Tuesday, carried a conversion premium of about 25 per cent, about 10 per centage points below the third-quarter average of 35 per cent, according to data from independent advisory firm Matthews South. Akamai issued two convertible bonds this week, each paying 1 per cent in interest, up from the average rate of 0.75 per cent in the third quarter.

"I was hoping for an adjustment like the one we had in the past couple of days," said Nicolo Bocchin, global head of fixed income at Azimut Group, referring to the steep selloff in AI companies last week. AFTER THE DELUGE Convertible bonds have been particularly attractive to technology companies because they allow firms to borrow at lower interest rates than conventional debt. They give investors the option of converting their debt to shares if the stock price rises above a predetermined level.  Pricing terms were skewed in favor of issuers during a deluge of issuance, much of it by AI players, in the first nine months of 2026, investors said. US convertible sales increased to about $153.6 billion by the end of October from $98.6 billion over the same period last year, according to data from Dealogic. "In the past few years, these deals were priced with premiums that I don't remember in history," said Bocchin. Alphabet sold $19 billion of converts in June and Oracle $5 billion in February, alongside repeated deals from neoclouds such as CoreWeave and Nebius.  "The convert market is quite disproportionately exposed to the AI narrative," said Venu Krishna, head of convertibles strategy at Barclays. About 70 per cent of the record issuance this year is AI-linked and 45 per cent is core AI infrastructure, he added. This isn't the first year in which terms loosened. In 2025, 46 convertible bond deals carried no interest, according to data from Matthews South, compared with 11 in 2024. DOSE OF SOBRIETY But questions about the sustainability of the AI boom have brought forth a reality check. The FTSE Russell US Convertible bonds index has fallen about 17.5 per cent from its all-time peak in June, leaving it up just under 2 per cent for the year. US convertibles lost more than 6 per cent last month, their worst October since 2008, Barclays data showed. "We got to a point where there were some frothy new issues being priced at levels that were fairly aggressive. And in these last couple of weeks, the market has responded to that," said Michael Barry, fixed income portfolio manager at Wellington Management. Buyers of convertible bonds have favored issuers outside data centers recently. Xcel Energy sold $2.2 billion of converts last week and fintech firm SS&C raised about $1 billion in an upsized deal. Both were trading above their offer prices, said Tracy Maitland, president and chief investment officer at Advent Capital Management. Eli Pars, co-chief investment officer and co-head of convertible strategies at Calamos Investments, said it was hard to predict when convertible volumes would bounce back. "But I haven't seen any reason why it should be coming from issuers other than those it's been coming from. That probably means more neocloud issuance."

Source: Reuters

Nov 12 : Anthropic is set to hold an IPO, giving the company a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, the latest affirmation of Wall Street's appetite for AI. The AI lab, best known for its Claude chatbot, and some of its investors are aiming to raise up to $64.4 billion by selling 825 million shares at as much as $78 per share. The company will also raise $26 billion via a separate private placement deal with cornerstone investors including Alphabet's Google, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices. SpaceX's $75 billion public offering in June was the biggest US IPO on record, dwarfing Alibaba, Visa and Facebook, now Meta Platforms. The charts below compare Anthropic with high-profile market debuts of the past on valuation and fundamentals.

Anthropic's owners are plowing ahead despite a recent selloff across the technology sector, as investors question the technology's likely returns and the likely impact of rising debt costs. "The timing of the IPO is notable because investors have become much more focused on the costs of the AI buildout than they were over the past few years," said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote Bank. "Political and regulatory uncertainties, along with a higher interest-rate environment, have also raised questions about future AI spending. As a result, many investors see Anthropic's IPO as an important test of appetite for AI-related investments."

Nov 12 : The European Space Agency has released its first big collection of data from the orbiting Euclid telescope's mission to map the universe's large-scale structure, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies, as scientists investigate the puzzling cosmic components dark matter and dark energy. The data unveiled on Thursday covered a survey of the sky equal to about 9,500 times the size of the moon as viewed from Earth. The mission's goal is to complete the largest-ever three-dimensional atlas of the cosmos, spanning more than a third of the sky, in 2031. Thursday's release encompassed around 13 months of Euclid observations, totaling an enormous 1.7 petabytes — 1.7 million gigabytes — of data. "It marks a major milestone for ESA's Euclid mission and for everyone involved," said astrophysicist Valeria Pettorino, ESA's Euclid project scientist.

Euclid, launched from Florida in 2023, is gathering data on how the universe has expanded and how its structure has formed over time while amassing information about the nature of dark energy and dark matter and the role of gravity on large scales. "Euclid will not just take images of galaxies in the sky, in two dimensions, but will also measure their distance, the third dimension. This will tell us where galaxies are in space and time, across 10 billion years, and in all directions beyond our galactic plane," Pettorino said. "Galaxies cluster along filaments, surrounded by empty space, and form a network that we call the cosmic web. Euclid will reconstruct the cosmic web and how it has grown over time. This is important because the exact configuration of the cosmic web, how many clusters or voids are there, how fast it changed, depend on the properties of dark energy and dark matter," Pettorino said. The universe's contents include ordinary matter as well as dark matter and dark energy. Ordinary matter — stars, planets, gas, dust and all the familiar stuff on Earth — represents about 5 per cent of the contents. Dark matter, known from the gravitational effects it exerts on galactic scales, is invisible material that may make up about 27 per cent of the cosmos. Dark energy, thought to be responsible for the accelerated expansion of the universe, may account for 68 per cent. Dark matter and dark energy do not emit or absorb light and cannot be directly observed. Previous Euclid data releases covered only a few days of observations. The newly released dataset includes more than a year of data and still spans only 14 per cent of the total sky area Euclid is due to survey in visible and near-infrared light over six years. This data release will be completed next year with the first results on dark energy and dark matter. GRAVITATIONAL LENSING Light traveling toward Earth from faraway galaxies can be bent and distorted by normal matter and dark matter in the foreground, an effect called gravitational lensing. Thus, the nearer galaxy's gravity warps the light coming from the one behind.     Gravitational lensing is one of the tools being used to study dark matter's distribution. The new Euclid data includes about 15,000 strong gravitational lens candidates, exceeding the total number discovered in the previous half century. "Gravitational lenses are nature's own weighing scales," said Natalie Lines, a doctoral student in astrophysics at the University of Portsmouth in England and a member of the Euclid Consortium of scientists. "How strongly the light is bent tells us how much matter a galaxy contains, including invisible components like dark matter. With thousands of lenses, we can study how dark matter is spread through galaxies and understand how galaxies form and evolve over cosmic time," Lines said. Lines noted the sharpness of the Euclid images over a huge area of the cosmos. "Telescopes on Earth can cover large areas of the night sky, but their view is blurred by the atmosphere. The Hubble and James Webb space telescopes take beautifully sharp images, but only of tiny patches of sky. Euclid does both at once, and that is crucial for finding things that are small and rare, like strong gravitational lenses," Lines said. Looking across vast distances means peering into the past because of the time needed for light from distant objects to reach us. The most distant objects Euclid has viewed are quasars, the brilliant cores of galaxies powered by supermassive black holes. The telescope has pinpointed 60 million of them. "Euclid has found some dating back to when the universe was just 5 per cent of its current age, so their light set off around 13 billion years ago," Lines said.

Source: Reuters

Nov 12 : Manchester United dismissed manager Michael Carrick on Thursday after a prolonged winless Premier League run culminated in a 4-4 draw against Aston Villa at Old Trafford last weekend, leaving the struggling team mired in the relegation zone. United have won only three of their 15 matches in all competitions under Carrick this season - including one league victory - leaving them 18th in the table on eight points after 10 games, one point from the bottom. "After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions," United said in a statement on their website. Carrick came under mounting pressure after a 3-0 home loss to Bournemouth and the former United midfielder carried the air of someone awaiting the inevitable after the defeat when fans chanted his name but booed the players off the pitch.

He had dropped captain Bruno Fernandes to the bench against Bournemouth and did not bring him on even when United were desperate for inspiration in midfield, but the struggling club gave Carrick another chance to revive their season. Although he restored the playmaker to the starting lineup against Chelsea following clear-the-air talks and spoke of the team's determination to put things right, little changed as they were comprehensively outplayed in a 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge. A 3-2 comeback win over AS Roma in the Champions League briefly eased the pressure on Carrick, but United's familiar defensive frailties were exposed again in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, despite two injury-time goals salvaging a point. CARRICK'S TENURE Carrick was appointed on an interim basis following Ruben Amorim's sacking in January before being handed a contract until 2028 after overseeing a turnaround in the side's fortunes. United won 11 of their first 16 matches under Carrick, including victories over Arsenal, Manchester City, Liverpool and Chelsea, to climb to third in the Premier League and secure qualification for the Champions League. The 45-year-old proved unable to carry that momentum into the new season, however, with United notching wins only against promoted Ipswich Town and Champions League debutants Sabah FK before embarking on a nine-match winless run. The club praised Carrick for his professional conduct during his managerial tenure, and said they were working towards appointing a permanent successor as soon as possible. He ultimately became another managerial casualty at Old Trafford after the reigns of David Moyes, Louis van Gaal, Jose Mourinho, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Erik ten Hag and Amorim. WHAT NEXT FOR UNITED? Carrick is likely to be replaced by Mauricio Pochettino, the US men's national team coach, who has agreed to take over the newly vacant post, according to reports in British media. The former Southampton, Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea manager is one of the Premier League's most highly regarded former coaches. United have not won the English league title since lifting the trophy for the 20th time in 2013 when Alex Ferguson left the club following a trophy-laden 27-year stint as manager. A daunting trip to Anfield to face rivals Liverpool awaits United after the international break. Pochettino is expected to remain in charge of the US for their upcoming CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final matches, which would leave the Argentine little time to prepare for his first game in one of English football's most demanding jobs.

Source: Reuters

BENGALURU, Nov 12 : India has launched an inquiry into how telecoms officials blocked websites based on forged court orders disclosed by Reuters, while police have sought ministry records as part of a criminal investigation, officials said on Thursday. An arm of the telecoms ministry this year directed internet providers to block 129 illegal betting websites, but Reuters revealed on Wednesday that the directives were based on forged orders issued in the names of two state high courts and emailed to officials by alleged fraudsters posing as lawyers. The findings have raised questions about safeguards in India's content-takedown system and prompted concerns that legitimate websites could be blocked using falsified court documents. The telecoms ministry's inquiry will review its procedures and consider additional checks before officials act on court orders seeking website takedowns, a government official with direct knowledge of the matter said.

"It's serious ... Maybe in future some genuine websites may also be blocked in the same manner," the official said. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the ministry was trying to identify those behind the email addresses used to send the forged orders, which were issued in the names of the Rajasthan and Allahabad high courts. The ministry plans to revoke the blocking directives issued on the basis of the forged orders and remove related documents from its website, the official added. As of Thursday, correspondence with the alleged fraudsters and copies of the forged orders remained available online. The telecoms ministry did not respond to queries. Reuters is first to report details of the government's response. CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION The case comes amid growing concern over fake and AI-generated legal material. India's Supreme Court in July struck down a tribunal ruling that relied on non-existent judgments, while a US judge in June disqualified lawyers over fabricated legal citations. Police opened a criminal investigation after checks by the Allahabad High Court found that one of the purported orders in its name cited by the ministry had not been issued by the court, according to police documents reviewed by Reuters. The document contained a fabricated court logo and seal, as well as a fake QR code, Reuters reported on Wednesday. Ghanshyam Yadav, a cybercrime official in Uttar Pradesh, said police had asked the telecoms ministry for details of its content management system and digital logs to understand how it processed the forged orders and help identify those responsible. The ministry's response would help determine the next steps in the investigation, he said, adding that police had sent 24 questions to the ministry. Since the Reuters report, politicians and activists have called for stronger verification of court orders before website takedowns are enforced. "(Why did the) ministry not even bother to verify the so-called court order ... Beyond scary," Saket Gokhale, an opposition politician, wrote on X.

Source: Reuters

PARIS: A bomb alert temporarily disrupted train services at Calais-Fréthun station in northern France on Thursday (Nov 12) morning, affecting both domestic and international rail travel. Train services resumed later on Thursday morning after the gendarmerie authorised their restart, national rail operator SNCF said. The national gendarmerie did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment. International high-speed rail operator Eurostar said some services between London and Paris had been affected by the disruption, as trains traveling on the route pass through Calais-Fréthun. The incident caused delays to services to and from London, the company said. The alert came amid a broader wave of bomb threats and hoaxes reported in France and other European countries in recent months, targeting flights, schools and, in some cases, media organisations. It was not immediately clear whether Thursday's alert was linked to any of the previous threats.

Nov 12 : England's highest wicket-taker James Anderson is set to continue his county cricket career with the 44-year-old fast bowler joining Surrey for the 2027 season, the club said on Thursday. Regarded as one of the greatest pace and swing bowlers of all time, Anderson took 991 wickets for England across all formats, a record for all fast bowlers. He retired from international cricket in 2024 and his 25-year spell at Lancashire came to an end last month after the club did not renew his contract. Anderson said he was shocked by his Lancashire exit but looked for new opportunities, culminating in his arrival at Surrey.
